title: Risk Register
summary: A risk register is the controlled record of identified risks that an organisation has decided to track, each entry capturing the risk statement, the affected assets and business processes, the threat and vulnerability that make it credible, the existing controls, the assessed likelihood and impact, the resulting inherent and residual rating, the risk owner, the treatment decision and the target date. It is the operational heart of a risk management programme because it converts assessment into accountable action: an entry without a named owner and a due date is an observation, not a managed risk. Practitioners should treat the register as a living engineering artefact rather than an annual spreadsheet. Good registers express risk in a consistent grammar such as cause, event and consequence, so that two analysts score similar situations similarly; they attach evidence such as detection coverage gaps, vulnerability findings, control test results and near-miss incident data; and they record risk acceptance explicitly, with the accepting authority, the rationale and the expiry. Risk scoring should be calibrated against real incident and loss data where it exists, because uncalibrated five-by-five matrices drift toward subjective optimism. Registers also need lifecycle discipline: risks are reviewed on a defined cadence, escalated when treatment slips, closed with evidence, and linked to the frameworks in use, whether ISO 27001 clause six, NIST SP 800-30 or a sector regulator's expectations. Effective registers are visible to engineering, not locked in a GRC tool only compliance staff can open.
objectives: You will be able to write risk statements in a consistent cause, event and consequence structure that different analysts score the same way.
You will be able to attach control evidence, detection coverage and vulnerability data to support likelihood and impact ratings.
You will be able to assign risk owners with authority to accept or treat, and set meaningful target dates.
You will be able to document formal risk acceptance with rationale, accepting authority and review expiry.
You will be able to run a review cycle that escalates overdue treatment and closes risks only with evidence.
You will be able to calibrate a risk matrix against incident and loss data rather than unfounded opinion.

beginner.definition: A risk register is a living list of the risks your organisation has decided to track. Each entry describes the risk, what it could harm, how likely it is and how bad it would be. It also names an owner and a treatment decision. Without those last parts, it is only a list of worries.
beginner.whyItMatters: Most organisations know their problems but nobody remembers who agreed to fix them. Work slips, priorities change and the same discussion returns every year. A register keeps the decision, the owner and the date in one place. It also shows auditors and leaders that you manage risk on purpose rather than by accident.
howItWorks: Write each risk in the same simple shape: cause, event and consequence.
Note which business processes and which computer systems the risk could damage.
Record the controls you already have and how well each one works.
Score the likelihood and impact, then give every entry a named owner.
Choose to treat, transfer, avoid or accept the risk, with a date.
Review the list on a schedule, escalate late work and close with evidence.
beginner.example: Think of a household repair list on the fridge. Writing down that the roof leaks is not enough. You add who will call the roofer, what it may cost and when it must be done. If you decide to live with the leak, you write that down too, so nobody reopens the argument. A risk register is that fridge list for the risks facing your systems.
takeaways: A risk without a named owner and a date is not managed.
Write risks the same way every time so scores stay comparable.
Record accepted risks openly, with the reason and a review date.

exercises.title: Risk Register - EASY
exercises.summary: Recall and recognition: definitions, one clear answer, single-step questions.

exercises.title: Risk Register - MEDIUM
exercises.summary: Application: read a short log or alert and choose the correct next step.

exercises.title: Risk Register - HARD
exercises.summary: Analysis: a multi-step scenario with distractors, evidence to weigh, and a reason to give.

exercises.title: Risk Register - EXTREMELY HARD
exercises.summary: Synthesis under pressure: incomplete evidence, competing priorities, and a decision you must defend.
